title: Whatever you do, offer it
hookLine: the women of Mathura envy the milkmaids who sang of Krishna while they churned; one verse turns the whole day into an offering
carry: arpana: every ordinary act can be offered
tomorrow: The robber who became a poet

lines: THEY SING OF HIM WHILE THEY CHURN.
cards: Krishna has grown up and left the cowherd village. In Mathura, the tyrant Kamsa sets him to wrestle the king's champions in a packed arena.
The women of the city watch from the stands, and the Bhagavata Purana gives them a line nobody expects. They don't envy the queens or the sages. They envy the milkmaids back in Vraja.
Lucky are they, the women say: while they milk the cows, pound the grain, churn the butter, sweep the floors and rock their crying babies, they sing about him. Their chores were already worship.

teach.b: Years later, on the battlefield, Krishna puts the same idea into one verse.
Verse twenty-seven: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give, whatever discipline you practice, Arjuna, do it as an offering to me.

In Sanskrit it's a list with a drumbeat: yat karoshi, whatever you do; yad ashnasi, whatever you eat; yaj juhoshi, whatever you offer into the fire; dadasi yat, whatever you give; yat tapasyasi, whatever effort you make.
Five whatevers, and one instruction: tat kurushva mad-arpanam, make it an offering to me. Look at the list.
Eating comes second, right next to sacrifice. Yesterday Krishna asked for a leaf. Today he asks for the whole day: not more stuff, more of your ordinary life, turned toward him.
They didn't stop churning to pray; the churning became the prayer.

teach.h: FREED FROM THE BONDS OF ACTION.
teach.b: Verse twenty-eight says what happens: you'll be freed from the bonds of action, with its good and bad fruits, and you'll come to me.
Some readers hear chapter three's work without attachment here: it's hard to clutch the fruit of something you've already given away.
This is arpana, offering, and it's why some families close a meal or a task with a quiet word: Krishnarpanam, offered to Krishna.

how: Many Hindus try to dedicate their daily work as an offering in the spirit of Gita 9.27; some sing or repeat God's name while they work, and some close a meal or a task with 'Krishnarpanam', offered to Krishna.

o: a fee paid to a temple priest
giving up eating for a day

games.q: the five whatevers — tap the pairs.

s: verse 27 only talks about temple rituals
it lists doing, eating, offering, giving and effort; eating is second on the list.
verse 28 says offering action frees you from its bonds
freed from the bonds of action with its good and bad fruits.
the women of Mathura envied the milkmaids of Vraja
they sang of Krishna while they milked, churned, swept and rocked their babies (Bhagavata 10.44).

games.q: you're a milkmaid in Vraja: butter to churn, a floor to sweep, a baby crying. how do the women of Mathura say you worship Krishna?
o: stop working and go find a temple.
sing of him while you churn and rock the baby.
wait until every chore is done.
games.why: they sang of him through the chores, so the chores became worship. Gita 9.27 says it outright: whatever you do, make it an offering.

practice: Pick one chore you'll do today: the dishes, the laundry, the walk to the bus. Do it the way the women of Vraja did, with a name, a song or a thought of God running underneath it.
If you pray, you can say at the end, as some families do, offered to Krishna. If not, simply do it with care, as if handing it to someone you love.

wordCard.voice: Arpana. Offering, handing over. Gita nine, twenty-seven: whatever you do, eat, offer, give or strive for, make it an offering.

orig.note: Sanskrit: mad-arpanam, as an offering to me; mat (me) + arpana (offering, handing over).

carryVoice: Your line: arpana, every ordinary act can be offered. The dishes too. Day one hundred ninety-one, offered.
